questions.scenario: Your team is given a new project. The goal is clear, but no one has decided how the work should be organized.

responses.text: Start on the portion you understand best and coordinate when your work begins to overlap with others.
Start a discussion about responsibilities and help the group settle on an approach before much work begins.
Wait briefly to see how the group naturally organizes itself, then fill whichever role seems most useful.
Develop an initial approach yourself and bring it to the group as something they can modify.

questions.scenario: A process you use regularly suddenly stops working during a busy period.

responses.text: Try several likely fixes immediately and keep moving unless one creates a larger problem.
Pause, identify what changed, and gather enough information to isolate the cause before altering anything.
Ask someone familiar with the process what they are seeing, then troubleshoot from there.
Create a temporary workaround so the work continues, then investigate the underlying problem afterward.

questions.scenario: Someone strongly disagrees with your recommendation in front of other people.

responses.text: Explain your reasoning directly and continue defending the recommendation unless new evidence changes your mind.
Ask them to walk through their reasoning before deciding whether the disagreement changes anything.
Let the discussion move on for the moment and revisit the issue privately if it still matters.
Shift the conversation toward the shared goal and try to build a version both sides can support.

questions.scenario: A newer teammate asks for help with something you could complete much faster yourself.

responses.text: Do it with them and explain your reasoning as you go, even though it takes longer.
Give them the key steps and let them try, staying available if they get stuck.
Complete the urgent part yourself, then explain it afterward when there is more time.
Point them toward the best resource and let them work through it independently.

questions.scenario: A plan you spent a lot of time preparing is rejected.

responses.text: Ask what would make it workable and start revising it while the feedback is fresh.
Take some time to process the disappointment before deciding what to do next.
Review the objections carefully and determine whether the original plan is still worth defending.
Move on quickly and build a different approach from scratch.

questions.scenario: A group conversation is quiet and no one seems willing to start.

responses.text: Open with a question that gives everyone an easy way into the discussion.
Wait; silence does not necessarily need to be filled.
Offer your own view first so others have something concrete to respond to.
Address one person you know has useful knowledge and invite their perspective.

questions.scenario: You notice someone close to you seems upset but says they are fine.

responses.text: Tell them you noticed and ask directly whether they want to talk.
Stay nearby and act normally, giving them room to bring it up themselves.
Do something practical that might make their day easier without asking for an explanation.
Accept what they said and avoid pushing unless their behavior suggests something more serious.

questions.scenario: You are responsible for a decision and the available information is incomplete.

responses.text: Choose the most reasonable option now and adjust later if necessary.
Delay the decision until you can reduce the biggest uncertainty.
Ask several people for their perspectives, then make the call.
Choose the option with the most reversible downside so you can act without locking yourself in.

questions.scenario: A routine that has worked for a long time is being replaced by a new system.

responses.text: Learn the new system early so you can figure out how to make it useful.
Keep using the old method until the new one proves it is actually better.
Switch when required, but preserve the parts of the old routine that still work.
Ask what problem the change is supposed to solve before deciding how much of your approach should change.

questions.scenario: You make a noticeable mistake that affects other people.

responses.text: Acknowledge it immediately, explain the correction, and fix what you can.
Fix the problem first and discuss it once you understand exactly what happened.
Tell the affected people, ask what they need from you, and coordinate the recovery.
Correct it quietly if possible and focus on preventing a repeat.

questions.scenario: You are overloaded and someone asks you to take on one more task.

responses.text: Say no clearly and explain what would need to move for you to take it on.
Accept it and reorganize your own workload to make room.
Ask how urgent it is and negotiate scope or timing before answering.
Take it if the person seems to need the help, even if it makes your schedule harder.

questions.scenario: Two people you work with are stuck in a disagreement that is slowing everyone down.

responses.text: Step in and help them identify the actual decision that needs to be made.
Let them work it out unless they specifically ask you to intervene.
Hear both sides separately before suggesting a path forward.
Set a temporary direction so work can continue and revisit the disagreement later.

questions.scenario: You receive criticism that feels unfair.

responses.text: Respond immediately and explain what you think the criticism is missing.
Ask for specific examples before deciding whether you agree.
Keep your reaction private until you have had time to think about it.
Focus on whatever part is useful and leave the rest alone.

questions.scenario: A friend or coworker repeatedly asks for advice but rarely follows it.

responses.text: Keep giving advice when asked; what they do with it is their choice.
Ask whether they actually want advice or just want someone to listen.
Stop offering detailed solutions unless they show they intend to act on them.
Tell them directly that the pattern is frustrating and ask what kind of help would be useful.

questions.scenario: You join a group where everyone already seems to know one another.

responses.text: Introduce yourself to a few people and start asking questions.
Stay observant until there is a natural opening to join a conversation.
Find one person who seems approachable and talk mostly with them at first.
Focus on the activity itself; relationships can develop if they need to.

questions.scenario: A deadline is approaching and the original plan is clearly no longer realistic.

responses.text: Cut lower-priority pieces and protect the most important outcome.
Push harder to complete the original plan as promised.
Bring the problem to the group and renegotiate what success should look like.
Rebuild the plan around what can realistically be finished, even if the method changes completely.

questions.scenario: You have been trying to solve a difficult problem alone and are making little progress.

responses.text: Keep working until you have exhausted the approaches you can think of.
Ask someone for help once you can clearly explain where you are stuck.
Show someone what you have so far and solve the remaining problem together.
Step away temporarily and return with a different approach before involving anyone else.

questions.scenario: Someone changes plans with you at the last minute.

responses.text: Adjust without much concern if the new plan still works.
Ask why the change happened before deciding whether you are okay with it.
Feel irritated but adapt rather than turning it into a conflict.
Say directly if the change creates a problem for you and work out another option.

questions.scenario: You realize a person has misunderstood something you said and is now upset.

responses.text: Clarify what you meant immediately, even if the conversation is uncomfortable.
First acknowledge how it sounded from their perspective, then explain what you meant.
Give them some space and revisit it after emotions settle.
Focus on repairing the practical problem rather than debating the wording.

questions.scenario: You are asked to lead something you have never done before.

responses.text: Accept and learn what you need as you go.
Accept, but first find someone experienced who can help you understand the risks.
Prefer to contribute without leading until you have more experience.
Build a basic plan, assign the first steps, and refine the approach once work starts.

questions.scenario: A person you care about is making a choice you strongly disagree with.

responses.text: Tell them exactly why you disagree, even if they may not like hearing it.
Ask questions until you understand why the choice makes sense to them.
Make your concern known once, then respect that the decision is theirs.
Offer practical help that reduces the risks without trying to control the decision.

questions.scenario: After a stressful failure, you have another important task the next day.

responses.text: Return to your normal routine and focus on the next task.
Review what went wrong while it is fresh, then make a specific adjustment for tomorrow.
Talk it through with someone you trust before trying to reset.
Give yourself time to feel bad about it, then re-engage when the emotion has settled.

questions.scenario: You discover a rule is producing a bad outcome in an unusual situation.

responses.text: Follow the rule for now and raise the issue through the proper channel.
Use judgment and make an exception if you can justify it.
Ask whoever owns the rule how they want the unusual case handled.
Find a solution that stays technically within the rule while avoiding the bad outcome.

questions.scenario: A group you are part of succeeds after a difficult stretch.

responses.text: Celebrate openly and make sure people know their work mattered.
Feel satisfied but prefer to move quietly into whatever comes next.
Call out the specific people or decisions that made the recovery possible.
Enjoy the result, then immediately start thinking about how to make the next attempt easier.
